The [starter](../../starters/mps2-an385-zephyr.md) made a west workspace for
Zephyr 3.7, scaffolded a Rust talker for `board = "mps2-an385-zephyr"`,
Zephyr's `mps2/an385` Cortex-M3 under QEMU, and heard it from ROS 2. This
page covers what comes after it: what is particular to the board, naming a
Zephyr board nano-ros does not ship, extending the build the Zephyr way, and
reading the run plan. Where an image's nano-ros and Zephyr settings go, one
image per RMW, and `nros build`'s hand-off to `west` are the same on every
Zephyr board; the [Zephyr native_sim](zephyr-native-sim.md) page covers
them.

## Configure the platform

The board's own configuration puts the image on QEMU's user-mode network:
its `prj.conf` gives the guest `10.0.2.15`, with gateway `10.0.2.2`, and the
locator `tcp/10.0.2.2:7447`. `nros build` applies it, so a scaffolded image
states nothing. The gateway is your host, so a router listening on the
host's `0.0.0.0:7447` is reachable, as the starter's was. An image whose
router listens elsewhere states its own `locator`:

```toml
[image.zephyr]
board = "mps2-an385-zephyr"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7800"
```

The image's other nano-ros settings (`rmw`, knobs, `os_config` fragments)
are the same keys as on every Zephyr board; see
[Configure the platform](zephyr-native-sim.md#configure-the-platform).

## Board notes

- **Zephyr's `mps2/an385` under QEMU.** The image uses Zephyr's own IP stack
  on the emulated SMSC911x ethernet. `nros run` boots it under the QEMU the
  Zephyr SDK ships, `qemu:mps2-an385`.
- **The west workspace needs nano-ros's patches for this board.**
  `nros setup board mps2-an385-zephyr --zephyr-workspace <ws>` applies them
  and adds the board's Rust target. Without them, zephyr-lang-rust's cargo
  command carries none of nano-ros's settings for the board, among them the
  C cross compiler the zenoh-pico crate builds with, and a Rust image fails
  to build.
- **Readiness.** Expect the first `Publishing:` line within about 15 seconds
  of boot: a cold QEMU boot and Zephyr's start-up come first.
- **Nothing is flashed.** `mps2/an385` is a QEMU machine. A Zephyr board
  you can hold, with a twin that boots the same image, is the
  [Nucleo-F767ZI](nucleo-f767zi.md) or the
  [Raspberry Pi Pico W](rpi-pico-w.md).

## Name a Zephyr board nano-ros does not ship

An image's `board` names a board in nano-ros's catalog, and the board's
descriptor states the Zephyr id `west build -b` receives. So an image writes
`board = "mps2-an385-zephyr"`, never `board = "mps2/an385"`: an image that
names a Zephyr id is refused with the id to write instead. A board the
catalog does not know is refused with the list of ones it does, because the
descriptor supplies more than the `-b` string: the platform, the toolchain
and the entry kind.

A board is a package. Put an `nros-board.toml` beside a package's
`package.xml` in your workspace, and it joins the catalog:

```toml
# src/my_board/nros-board.toml
[[board]]
names = ["my-board"]              # what your images say
west_board = "qemu_cortex_m3"     # what west is given
platform = "zephyr"
toolchain = "stable"
platform_feature = "platform-zephyr"
link_kind = "none"
entry_kind = "zephyr-staticlib"
```

Then an image names it, `board = "my-board"`, and builds for it. For a
board shared by several workspaces, list directories shaped like
`packages/boards/` in `$NROS_EXTRA_BOARD_PATH`. `nros new board <name>
--for-platform zephyr` scaffolds the descriptor. That is nano-ros's
descriptor only: an out-of-tree Zephyr board definition (its devicetree and
`board.yml`) comes in the Zephyr way, through your module's `board_root`.
[Add a board](../../extending/add-a-board.md) takes a board through the
rest, and [Flash a real board](flash-a-real-board.md) flashes it.

## Extend the build the Zephyr way

`nros build` runs a plain `west build`, so every Zephyr extension point is
untouched. The first row edits the application's `CMakeLists.txt`, so it
needs an application you own (`nros materialize <image>`); the rest do not:

| You want | You do |
| --- | --- |
| an out-of-tree module | `list(APPEND ZEPHYR_EXTRA_MODULES <dir>)` before `find_package(Zephyr)` |
| a driver in that module | `zephyr_library()` and `zephyr_library_sources()`, behind your own Kconfig |
| its devicetree binding | `dts/bindings/`, with `settings: {dts_root: .}` in the module's `zephyr/module.yml` |
| an out-of-tree board, SoC or snippet | the matching `board_root`, `soc_root` or `snippet_root` in that `module.yml` |
| your Kconfig on for one image | a `.conf` fragment in the image's `os_config`, passed as `EXTRA_CONF_FILE` |
| a devicetree overlay for one image | an `.overlay` in the same list, passed as `EXTRA_DTC_OVERLAY_FILE` |

Only the last two rows are nano-ros's, and they are how an image differs
from its siblings:

```toml
[image.zephyr]
board = "mps2-an385-zephyr"
os_config = ["prj-user-extra.conf", "user-widget.overlay"]
```

There is no image key for arbitrary `-D` defines: something the
application always needs belongs in its `CMakeLists.txt`. A mistake in your
module surfaces as Zephyr's own error, unchanged, because the build is a
plain `west build`.

## Read the run plan

From the starter's workspace, print the plan `nros run` follows:

```bash probe=410 track=installed
nros run zm_node --dry-run --why
```

The plan names the QEMU runner and the `qemu:mps2-an385` machine, the
console, and the link to the router the board's configuration names.
`--why` names where each fact came from.

## Drive west yourself

Print the `west build` line `nros build` runs, with the image's overlays,
without building:

```bash probe=420 track=installed
nros build --dry-run
```

[Drive west yourself](zephyr-native-sim.md#drive-west-yourself) explains
what goes to west and what is refused.

## If it doesn't work

1. Confirm the router listens on the host's `0.0.0.0` at the image's port.
   A router on `127.0.0.1` is unreachable from the guest.
2. A Rust image that fails to build naming its C compiler or target: run
   `nros setup board mps2-an385-zephyr --zephyr-workspace <ws>` again.
3. No `Publishing:` line within 30 seconds of boot: check the console for
   the network coming up, then [Troubleshoot](../deploy/troubleshoot.md).
